blocks.passage:
Business culture varies enormously between countries, and much of the variation is invisible until someone breaks an unwritten rule. How direct can you be in disagreement? How quickly is it acceptable to start negotiating? How important is small talk before the real conversation? Every culture answers these differently, and none of them are wrong.

The most useful attitude is curiosity over judgement. When something feels strange, assume there is a reason, and ask. In Japan, for example, silence at the table is significantly more comfortable than in Brazil. In Germany, a direct "this won't work" is far more acceptable than in the UK, where it would probably arrive as "I wonder if we might consider another angle."

Stereotypes have their limits. Every country has introverts and extroverts, direct people and diplomatic ones. Cultural awareness is a starting point, not a script.

items.q: According to the text, when does cultural variation usually become visible?
options: When someone breaks an unwritten rule
items.why: "much of the variation is invisible until someone breaks an unwritten rule."

items.q: What attitude does the text recommend?
items.why: "The most useful attitude is curiosity over judgement."

items.q: How is a direct "this won't work" likely to be expressed in the UK?
options: As "I wonder if we might consider another angle"
items.why: "in the UK, where it would probably arrive as 'I wonder if we might consider another angle.'"

items.q: What does the text say about stereotypes?
options: They have limits — every country has all kinds of people
items.why: "Stereotypes have their limits. Every country has introverts and extroverts."

items.q: "Cultural awareness is a starting point, not a script" means it should…
options: guide you, but not replace paying attention to the individual
items.why: Inferência: a consciência cultural orienta, mas não substitui olhar para a pessoa real.

audio.text:
Before we go into the Tokyo meeting, let me share what I've prepared, because the style here is quite different from what we're used to.

First, silence. There will be pauses that feel long to us. I'm not going to rush to fill them — in Japan, silence at the table is far more comfortable than back home, and it often means someone is thinking carefully, not that something's wrong.

Second, directness. I won't open with a blunt 'this doesn't work for us'. That lands as significantly more aggressive here than it would in Germany. I'll raise concerns as questions instead, so nobody loses face in front of their team.

Third, hierarchy. I'll let the most senior person speak first and I'll address my main points to them, even if a junior colleague is doing the detailed talking.

And I'll do more small talk than feels natural before we get to business. Rushing to the deal would signal that I only care about the transaction, not the relationship — and this is a relationship business.

items.q: How will James handle the long pauses in the meeting?
options: Not rush — silence is more comfortable there and often means thinking
items.why: "I'm not going to rush to fill them — in Japan, silence at the table is far more comfortable."

items.q: How will James raise concerns?
options: As questions, so nobody loses face
items.why: "I'll raise concerns as questions instead, so nobody loses face."

items.q: What does James say about directness compared with Germany?
options: A blunt line lands as significantly more aggressive in Tokyo than in Germany
It is more accepted in Tokyo
items.why: "That lands as significantly more aggressive here than it would in Germany."

items.q: How will James handle hierarchy?
options: Address the junior doing the detail
Let the most senior speak first and address main points to them
items.why: "I'll let the most senior person speak first and I'll address my main points to them."

items.q: Why will James do more small talk than feels natural?
options: Because rushing to the deal would signal he only cares about the transaction
Because it is required by law
items.why: "Rushing to the deal would signal that I only care about the transaction, not the relationship."

items.q: "He broke an **unwritten rule**." An unwritten rule is…
options: an accepted norm that isn't written down
items.why: Unwritten rule = regra não escrita.

items.q: "**Face-saving** matters in that culture." Face-saving means…
items.why: Face-saving = preservar a imagem/dignidade de alguém.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "There's a strong **___** here — the senior person speaks first."
items.why: Hierarchy = hierarquia.

items.q: "That's a **stereotype**." A stereotype is…
options: an oversimplified idea about a whole group
items.why: Stereotype = estereótipo, generalização simplista.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "There's a **___** in how the two teams handle disagreement."
items.why: Nuance = nuance, diferença sutil.

items.q: "Let's not **step on anyone's toes**." To step on someone's toes means to…
items.why: Step on someone's toes = pisar no calo, invadir a área de alguém.

items.q: "I don't want to **come across as** rude." To come across as means to…
items.why: Come across as = passar a impressão de.

items.q: "Let's **feel our way** carefully in the first meeting." To feel your way means to…
options: proceed cautiously, learning as you go
items.why: Feel your way = ir com cautela, tateando o terreno.

items.q: "They tend to **hold back** until they know you." To hold back means to…
items.why: Hold back = conter-se, ser reservado.

items.q: "Small talk helps you **build rapport**." To build rapport means to…
items.why: Build rapport = criar sintonia, boa relação.
